title: Shopping & money
goal: Ask prices, point out 'this one' and 'that one', try things on, bargain politely and pay.
intro:
Telugu has a beautifully regular set of 'pointing' words: everything near starts with **i-/ī-** (ఇది this, ఇక్కడ here, ఇప్పుడు now), everything far with **a-/ā-** (అది that, అక్కడ there, అప్పుడు then), and the question words with **e-/ē-** (ఏది which, ఎక్కడ where, ఎప్పుడు when).

Bargaining is normal in markets and small shops (not in malls or supermarkets). Keep it friendly: *కొంచెం తగ్గించండి* ('reduce it a little').

phrases.en: Bring the price down a little.

grammar.title: This and that: the i-/a-/e- system
grammar.body:
Near things begin with **ఇ/ఈ**, far things with **అ/ఆ**, questions with **ఎ/ఏ**:
ఈ (this) · ఆ (that) · ఏ (which) — before a noun
ఇది (this one) · అది (that one) · ఏది (which one)
ఇవి (these) · అవి (those) · ఏవి (which ones)
ఇతను / ఈయన (this man) · అతను / ఆయన (that man) · ఈమె / ఆమె (this/that woman) · వీళ్ళు / వాళ్ళు (these/those people)
ఇక్కడ / అక్కడ / ఎక్కడ (here, there, where) · ఇలా / అలా / ఎలా (like this, like that, how) · ఇంత / అంత / ఎంత (this much, that much, how much)

Before case endings, ఇది/అది become **దీని / దాని**: *దీని ధర* (this one's price), *దాని కంటే* (than that).

examples.en: This one's nice; I don't want that one.
What's the price of this one?

grammar.title: Prices and bargaining
grammar.body:
Ask **ఎంత?** (how much?) or **దీని ధర ఎంత?** The price you pay 'for' something takes the dative **-కి**: *ఎంతకి ఇస్తారు?* (for how much will you give it?), *వంద రూపాయలకి ఇవ్వండి* (give it for a hundred).

Hundreds: *వంద* (100) becomes **నూట** before another number (*నూట యాభై*, 150), and **వందల** in combinations (*రెండు వందల యాభై*, 250). Thousands: *వెయ్యి* (1000), *రెండు వేలు* (2000), *రెండు వేల ఐదు వందలు* (2500).

examples.en: How much is a kilo of tomatoes?
How much will you sell this for?
It's very expensive, bring it down a bit.

dialogue.title: Buying a sari
dialogue.setting: Padma is shopping for a cotton sari in a small shop in a market.

lines.speaker: Shopkeeper
lines.en: Come in, madam, what would you like?

lines.speaker: Padma
lines.en: Show me some cotton saris, please.

lines.speaker: Shopkeeper
lines.en: Look at these. These are new designs.

lines.speaker: Padma
lines.native: ఆ నీలం చీర బాగుంది. దాని ధర ఎంత?
lines.roman: ā nīlam chīra bāgundi. dāni dhara enta?
lines.en: That blue sari is nice. What's its price?

lines.speaker: Padma
lines.en: That's very expensive. Bring it down a bit.

lines.speaker: Shopkeeper
lines.native: ఇది మంచి క్వాలిటీ మేడం. వెయ్యి రూపాయలకి ఇస్తాను.
lines.roman: idi manchi kvāliṭī mēḍam. veyyi rūpāyalaki istānu.
lines.en: This is good quality, madam. I'll give it for a thousand.

lines.speaker: Padma
lines.en: Give it to me for eight hundred.

lines.speaker: Shopkeeper
lines.en: Nine hundred. It can't go lower than this.

lines.speaker: Padma
lines.en: Okay, I'll take it. Do you take cards?

culture: Andhra Pradesh and Telangana are famous for handloom saris: **Pochampally** ikat, **Gadwal**, **Venkatagiri**, **Dharmavaram** silk and **Mangalagiri** cotton. Shopkeepers address customers as *సార్* and *మేడం* (or *అమ్మా*, *అన్నా*), and in markets bargaining is expected, though fixed-price shops will politely refuse. Today most small payments, even at vegetable stalls, are made by scanning a UPI QR code with a phone.
